blocks.text: Two men can stop your bus on the same road at night. One wears a police uniform and shows a warrant card; the other holds a cutlass. Both have the power to make you stop. Only one of them has authority. That single difference is where the study of government begins.

blocks.markdown:
**Power** is the ability to make others behave as you wish, whether or not they agree. It rests on capacity — the strength, wealth, weapons, office or knowledge that lets you get your way. Power can be exercised legitimately or illegitimately.

Power is not one single thing. It appears in several forms in political life:

- **Political power** — the ability to make and enforce binding decisions for a community.
- **Coercive or military power** — the ability to compel by force or the threat of it.
- **Economic power** — the ability to control others through wealth, employment or credit.
- **Legislative power** — the ability to make law.
- **Persuasive power** — the ability to change minds through argument or reputation.

blocks.title: Authority
blocks.text: The recognised right to exercise power. Authority is power clothed in legitimacy: those subject to it accept the command as rightful and obey voluntarily, without needing to be forced.

blocks.markdown:
### Influence

**Influence** is the ability to affect the decisions of others without any right to command and usually without force. A respected traditional ruler, a popular musician, a newspaper columnist or a wealthy party financier may all influence what a government does, yet none of them can issue a lawful order.

The crucial test is this: authority commands and expects obedience as of right; influence persuades and can be ignored without penalty.

blocks.markdown:
### Max Weber's three types of authority

The German sociologist Max Weber classified authority by the reason people accept it.

1. **Traditional authority** rests on long-established custom and inheritance. An Emir, an Obi or an Oba holds authority because the throne has passed down that way for generations.
2. **Charismatic authority** rests on the exceptional personal qualities of the leader — courage, oratory, vision. Followers obey the person, not the office, so this authority is unstable and rarely outlives its holder.
3. **Legal-rational authority** rests on rules. A Nigerian Local Government Chairman is obeyed because the Constitution and the Electoral Act say that whoever wins that election holds that office and may issue those directives. The authority belongs to the office, not the person, and ends the day the person leaves office.

blocks.title: Classifying authority in a scenario
blocks.prompt: In a Nigerian town, three people give instructions on the same morning: the Emir orders the annual Durbar procession route; a newly elected Local Government Chairman orders the closure of an illegal dump site; a youth leader whose speeches inspire thousands asks young people to join a clean-up. Classify the authority in each case.

steps.text: Ask what makes each instruction acceptable to those who obey it.
The Emir's order is accepted because the stool has directed such ceremonies for centuries. Basis: custom and inheritance, so traditional authority.
The Chairman's order is accepted because the Constitution and an election placed him in an office empowered to make it. Basis: rules and office, so legal-rational authority.
The youth leader's request is accepted because of his personal magnetism. He holds no office and cannot punish refusal, so this is charismatic authority shading into mere influence.
Note the test that separates the third case: if disobedience carries no lawful penalty, you are looking at influence rather than authority.

blocks.answer: Emir — traditional authority; Local Government Chairman — legal-rational authority; youth leader — charismatic authority operating largely as influence

blocks.title: Answering the classic question
blocks.text: "Distinguish between power and authority" is asked almost every year. Do not merely define both. Draw the distinction on named grounds — legitimacy, source, and whether obedience is voluntary — and finish with a paired example such as the armed robber and the police officer. That structure secures the marks.

points: Power is the ability to control the behaviour of others, with or without their consent.
Authority is the legitimate right to exercise power, so obedience to it is voluntary.
Influence affects decisions without any right to command and can be ignored without penalty.
Max Weber identified traditional, charismatic and legal-rational authority.
Legal-rational authority attaches to the office rather than the person, which is why it survives a change of officeholder.
